why_angle: The cited rivals only say the 30 W Anker Nano is 'not the best' for iPhone 18 Pro. None of them states Apple's rule for that phone's top wired tier (a 60W-capable charger with AVS on USB-PD 3.2), and none names a charger under $20 that claims to meet it. This page checks each charger under $20 against that rule and against the PPS ceilings that limit Galaxy and Pixel phones.

page.title: Best USB-C Phone Charger Under $20 (2026): Watts, PPS and AVS Compared
page.desc: Which USB-C phone charger under $20 gives the most watts, and which supports the PPS and AVS modes Samsung and iPhone 18 Pro need. Prices read 2026-11-27.
page.answer: Short answer. The best USB-C phone charger under $20 is the Anker Nano Charger Neo: up to 65 W from one port, PPS, and the AVS mode Apple asks for to give iPhone 18 Pro its 60 W tier, which Anker says it supports and 30W chargers lack. UGREEN's Nexode Air 45W costs less.

page.after:
Why $20 is the line: TechGearLab's comparison lists Apple's own 20 W USB-C adapter at $19, so $20 buys a basic phone-only charger. On 2026-11-27 Black Friday prices bring 45–65 W chargers under that line. The Anker Nano Charger Neo is $15.99 on Anker's US store (compare-at $25.99), and UGREEN's Nexode Air 45W is {price:ugreen-nexode-air-45w-gan-charger} on UGREEN's US store (compare-at $24.99). Both are under $20 only at these sale prices, and neither store gives an end date. The Anker Nano 30W ($15.99 on Anker's store) and Belkin's 30W ($14.99 on Belkin's store, no strikethrough) are under the line at the makers' prices. One charger just misses it: UGREEN's Nexode Air 65W at {price:ugreen-nexode-air-65w-gan-charger}, which Charge-Test measured with AVS on its 'Version 3' unit. The rows are ranked by the watts one port gives one phone, then by whether the charger speaks the mode the phone needs (AVS, PPS), then by price. Dealectric does not test units. Every figure below names whose it is.

What the differences mean

  • Nano Charger Neo: 20 V × 3.25 A = 65 W on a 5 A cable, and 20 V × 3 A = 60 W on a 3 A cable (USB Connection Information's read of its profiles). Its measured draw into a MacBook Air M5 was 19 V × 3.15 A = 59.8 W. Anker says it lowers power after about 20 minutes at 65 W.
  • Nexode Air 45W: 20 V × 2.25 A = 45 W fixed. Its PPS ceiling is 11 V × 4.5 A = 49.5 W, so the 45 W rating is the real limit. smartzone.de saw 45 W drop to 40 W after 30 minutes: 5 ÷ 45 = 11% less.
  • Nano 30W: 20 V × 1.5 A = 30 W. Its top PPS step is 16 V × 2 A = 32 W, capped at 30 W. TechGearLab measured 29.4 W, and Android Authority measured 27 W over PPS.
  • Dollars per watt at the makers' prices: Neo 15.99 ÷ 65 = $0.25 (15.99 ÷ 45 = $0.36 once it settles); Nexode Air 45W 15.19 ÷ 45 = $0.34; Belkin 14.99 ÷ 30 = $0.50; Nano 30W 15.99 ÷ 30 = $0.53.

iPhone 18 Pro's 60 W tier: AVS decides it, not watts

Apple's support page lists two ways to charge an iPhone 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max to about 50% in about 15 minutes. One is Apple's 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max. The other is a third-party adapter that is 60W-capable, uses Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) and supports USB-PD 3.2. A 30 W charger misses that line on watts whatever modes it supports. The Nexode Air 45W misses it too, even though smartzone.de reports it supports SPR AVS.

The Nano Charger Neo is the only charger here whose maker claims both. Anker's Canadian product page says it “supports AVS charging and delivers up to 60W for iPhone 18 Pro, reaching 50% in 15 minutes”. USB Connection Information read the box label as AVS 9–15 V at 4.3 A and 15–20 V at 3.25 A. There are three limits. No named reviewer has measured it on an iPhone 18 Pro. The MacBook that Connection Info tested with negotiated USB PD 3.0, so AVS did not show there. And Anker's spec sheet lists PD3.1, not the 3.2 Apple names. Check the model number when you buy: Anker's FAQ says AVS and PPS belong to the A120M, and the A121D Nano Charger (45W, Smart Display) is a different model. {buy:anker-nano-charger-neo-a120m}

For Galaxy and Pixel phones the deciding figure is the PPS ceiling. All four chargers stop at 11 V or 16 V, so none gives the 20 V PPS that the Galaxy S26 Ultra's 60 W mode needs. For the 45 W class, smartzone.de expects 40–45 W from the Nexode Air 45W on recent Samsung PPS phones. That is a reviewer's estimate, not a measurement, and the same test read 71 °C on the housing under sustained load. {buy:ugreen-nexode-air-45w-gan-charger}

Not recommended

Belkin's 30W Compact charger is not a good pick for a Galaxy or Pixel owner. Belkin's own page lists USB-C PD 3.1 but no PPS and no voltage table, so you cannot count on Samsung's PPS fast-charge mode. For an iPhone 17e or iPhone Air, which Apple says need 20 W or more, it is fine. Android owners spending about the same should buy the Nano 30W, whose maker table lists PPS to 16 V.
